```markdown
---
name: scheduling-across-time-zones
description: "Book meetings and send invites to outside guests in the guest's time zone, not the agent's or owner's. Use whenever a task creates, moves or confirms a calendar event with someone outside the owner's organization."
---

# Scheduling Across Time Zones

## Why this matters
An invite that shows the wrong local time makes the guest arrive early, late or not at all. Last month, 9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours, and two customers missed calls. Every guest invite must show the time in the guest's own zone, and the event must be stored correctly in the owner's calendar.

## Before you book
1. Find the guest's time zone. Check, in this order: the time zone the guest stated in their email or message, the time zone on their CRM record, and the location in their email signature. If none of these is clear, ask the owner or the guest before booking. Do not assume it matches the owner's zone.
2. Find the owner's calendar time zone in the calendar settings. Write it down for this booking. Do not rely on the zone of the computer or server you are running on.
3. Write the proposed meeting as a pair: the owner's zone and the guest's zone, each with its date and time. Example: "Tue 14 Oct, 10:00 Pacific (owner) / 13:00 Eastern (guest)."
4. Check for daylight saving changes between now and the meeting date. The owner's zone and the guest's zone may not change on the same day, and the gap between them can shift by an hour.

## Creating the event
1. Create the event with an explicit time zone attached to the start and end times. Never create a bare local time without a zone.
2. Set the event's zone to the owner's calendar zone. The event is stored once, on the owner's calendar.
3. Add the guest as an attendee. Most calendar systems convert the time to each attendee's zone automatically, but only if the zone was attached in step 1.
4. Do not change the owner's calendar zone to match the guest's. Changing it moves every other event.

## Writing the invite text
1. In the body of any email or message to the guest, state the time in the guest's zone first, with the zone name and date. Add the owner's zone in brackets.
   Example: "Tuesday, 14 October, 1:00 PM Eastern Time (10:00 AM Pacific for [Owner])."
2. Include the full date. Do not write "Tuesday" alone.
3. Include the zone abbreviation or name, such as "EDT" or "Eastern Time." Do not write only "ET," since it is ambiguous.

## Verifying before you send
1. Open the event as the guest would see it, or use the calendar's preview of attendee time, and confirm the start time shows the guest's zone and the correct hour.
2. Compare the time in the message body against the time in the calendar. They must match exactly.
3. Check the date too. A time can be right on the wrong day when a meeting crosses midnight between zones.
4. If anything does not match, stop, correct the event, and do not send the message until the two agree.

## After a change
1. When a meeting is moved, repeat the full process above with the new time. Do not just change the hour in the calendar.
2. Send the updated time to the guest and cancel the old invite so there are not two events on the guest's calendar.

## When you cannot confirm
1. If the guest's zone is unknown, or the owner's zone is missing, do not create the event. Ask the owner first.
2. Keep a short note in the event description with both zones, so anyone reading it later can see which time was intended.
```

description: Book meetings with outside guests in the guest's time zone, check the invite before sending, and stop to ask when the guest's zone is unknown. Use whenever you create or move a calendar invite for someone outside the owner's organization.

# Book Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

## The mistake this fixes
Agents book meetings in their own or the owner's time zone. The guest then arrives one to three hours early or late. In one recent month, 9 of 20 outside invites were off this way, and two customers missed calls.

## Steps
1. Before choosing a time, find the guest's time zone. Check in this order: a time zone or city the guest wrote in their message, a time zone or city in their email signature, the time zone on their contact record. Note which source you used.
2. If none of these gives a clear zone, stop and ask the owner: "What time zone is [guest name] in?" Do not assume the owner's zone. Do not guess from the guest's email domain or phone number.
3. Convert the proposed slot into the guest's zone. Check that it falls within their working hours (roughly 08:00 to 18:00 local). If it doesn't, propose another slot.
4. Create the invite with the time zone set explicitly to the guest's zone. Do not rely on the calendar's default.
5. In the message body, write the time in both zones with zone names, for example: "Tuesday 14 March, 10:00 Pacific / 13:00 Eastern."
6. Before sending, reopen the saved invite and confirm the start time displays in the guest's zone as the same time you wrote in the message. If it doesn't, fix it before sending.
7. Record in your notes: guest name, zone, source of the zone, final start time.

## Stop and ask when
- The guest's zone isn't stated anywhere you can see.
- Two sources give different zones.
- The guest's zone is different from the owner's and the owner has told you to use one zone for everything.
- The guest is in a zone that changes its clocks during the proposed week and you can't confirm the date of the change.

## Never
- Send an invite whose start time you haven't checked against the guest's zone.
- Assume the owner's zone or the calendar's default zone is the guest's.
- Give a meeting time without naming its zone.
- Change an existing invite's zone without telling the owner and the guest.

```
# Pull Refunds to a Spreadsheet

Refund exports often double-count, miss refunds at the month edge, or mix test and live data. Each error throws off the books.
```

```markdown
description: "Export last month's refunds from the payment processor into a reconciliation spreadsheet. Use when preparing monthly refund reports or reconciling refunds against bank deposits."

# Pulling Monthly Refunds to a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Get an API key from your processor's dashboard with read-only access to refunds. Store it in your secrets manager or as an environment variable such as `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`. Never paste it into a script, spreadsheet, chat message or repository.
2. Confirm the reporting period. For "last month," use the first day to the last day of the previous calendar month in the account's time zone.
3. Decide whether you're working in live or sandbox mode. Use sandbox for practice and live only for real reconciliation.

## Steps
1. Request all refunds with a `created_at` date inside the reporting period. Follow pagination until the response has no next-page cursor, or you will miss records.
2. For each refund, keep these fields: refund ID, original charge ID, refund date, amount, currency, status, and reason code.
3. Mask payment details. Keep only the card brand and last four digits, shown as `XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-1234`. Do not export full card numbers, CVVs or customer bank details.
```

```
7. Never edit a PO or receipt to make an invoice match.

## Negotiating payment terms
1. Start from the current terms, the vendor's account history, and the owner's stated goal (for example, net 45 instead of net 30).
2. Prepare a short proposal: the request, the reason, and what the business offers in return, such as steady volume or a record of on-time payment.

4. Do not send a proposal, accept a change, or sign anything without the owner's written approval.
5. After agreement, confirm the new terms in writing, update the vendor record, and set reminders for the new due dates.
6. Never share other vendors' prices, the owner's cash position, or internal approval limits with a vendor.

## Reporting
1. End each reconciliation run with a summary of paid, held, and disputed invoices, each with amount and vendor, plus any open questions.
2. Flag any invoice above the owner's threshold, and any unexpected vendor change, for personal review.
```

description: "Book meetings and send calendar invites so each guest sees the correct local time. Use whenever an agent creates, moves or confirms a meeting with someone outside the owner's time zone."
---

# Scheduling Across Time Zones

## Core rule
A meeting time belongs to the guest's local clock. Set every invite in the guest's time zone, and never assume the calendar's default or the owner's zone is correct for an outside guest.

## Before booking
1. Find the guest's time zone. Check these sources in order and use the first one that is clear:
   a. The guest's time zone field in the CRM contact record.
   b. A time zone the guest stated in the email thread, such as "I'm in Chicago" or "Lisbon time."
   c. A city or region in their email signature or company address. Map it to a zone, and note that you inferred it.
2. If none of these settle it, ask the guest before booking: "What time zone are you in so I can send you the right time?" Do not guess and do not default to the owner's zone.
3. Record the zone you used and where it came from in the booking note.

## Creating the invite
1. Set the event's time zone to the guest's zone. In most calendar tools this is a "time zone" option on the event, separate from the owner's display setting. Confirm it is set before you save.
2. Confirm the date as well as the time. Some zones are a full day ahead of the owner's, so a 9:00 a.m. meeting can fall on a different calendar date.
3. Use the zone's offset on the actual meeting date, not a standard offset. Daylight saving changes can shift the gap by an hour for part of the year, and some regions do not observe it at all.

## Writing the invite text
Include both times in the description so the guest can check at a glance:

> Tuesday, 14 May, 10:00 a.m. Pacific (your time) / 1:00 p.m. Eastern (Owner's time)

Put the guest's time first. Name the zone with its abbreviation or city.

## Verifying before you send
1. Open the invite as the guest would see it, or read the time out of the invite's saved zone and compare it to what you told the guest.
2. Check that the zone on the invite matches the zone in your booking note.
3. If the owner's calendar shows the meeting at a time that looks odd for them, do not change it to fit. The invite is for the guest. Check that the owner's calendar entry is correct for the owner's zone.

## Moving or confirming meetings
1. When rescheduling, repeat the full check above. Never change only the date or the hour.
2. In reminders and confirmations, restate the time in the guest's zone.
3. If a guest's zone changes mid-thread (travel, relocation), update the CRM record and ask them to confirm the meeting time.

## When to escalate
Tell the owner before sending if:
- The guest's zone cannot be determined and the guest has not replied.
- The meeting falls in a window that is unusual for the guest, such as before 7 a.m. or after 9 p.m. local time.
- The guest is in a zone that changes its clock on a day close to the meeting.

## Checking after a booking
At the end of each week, review the invites created and confirm each one shows the guest's zone. Note any that do not, and fix them before the meeting date.

---

- I'd recommend adding a checklist version of "Before booking" and "Verifying before you send" to the agents' setup, since those are the steps most likely to be skipped.

1. One row per refund ID. Before appending, check whether that ID is already in the sheet. If it is, skip it and log it. Never add a row twice.
2. Keep amounts exactly as the processor gives them, in the currency's smallest unit or as decimals. Don't round.
3. Mask card data: keep only the card brand and last four digits, and only if the sheet needs them. Never copy full card numbers, keys or tokens.
4. Copy customer names as the processor shows them. Don't infer a name from an email address.

Example row (test values): refund ID re_TEST_001, Test Customer A, Visa ending 0000, 12.50, 2025-03-14, succeeded.

- The sum of refund amounts in the sheet equals the processor's total for the month.
- The number of rows equals the number of refund IDs exported.
- No blank IDs, dates or amounts.

If a check fails, stop and report the difference. Don't edit values to make the totals match.

## 5. Stop and ask when
- The processor total and the exported total differ.
- A refund is in a currency other than the business's.
- You can't tell whether a refund belongs to this month or a neighbouring one.
- You need access, a key or a login you weren't given.

## 6. Never
- Put live API keys, passwords, tokens or full card numbers in the sheet, in a message, or in any catalog file.
- Issue, cancel or edit a refund while exporting. This job only reads.

```
---
name: book-meetings-in-guest-time-zone
description: "Book meetings with outside guests in the guest's own time zone, confirm the zone before sending, and stop to ask when it is unknown or conflicting. Use when scheduling or sending invites for any meeting with a guest who is not on the owner's team."

# Book Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

## The mistake
Scheduling agents book outside meetings in the owner's or the agent's own time zone. In a recent month, 9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours, and two customers missed calls. The calendar shows the wrong time as if it were right, so the error is easy to miss.

## Steps
1. Before choosing a time, find the guest's time zone. Check these sources in order:
   a. The guest's own words: a stated zone, a zone abbreviation, or a city.
   b. Their email signature or address block.
   c. The time zone field on the CRM contact record.
   d. A past meeting with them on the calendar.
2. If no source gives a zone you can rely on, stop and ask the owner before booking. Do not default to the owner's zone.
3. If sources disagree, stop and ask. Do not guess which one is right.
4. Convert the proposed time to the guest's zone and check the local hour. Unless the guest asked for it, avoid times before 8:00 or after 18:00 local. If the hour fails, propose another time.
5. Create the invite with its time zone set explicitly to the guest's zone, not the calendar's default.
6. In the invite and in your message, state the time in both zones, with the zone name and UTC offset for that date. Example: "Tuesday 14 March, 10:00 AM Pacific (UTC-7) / 1:00 PM Eastern (UTC-4)." Daylight saving can change the offset, so use the one that applies on the meeting date.
7. Before sending, reread the invite. Check that the guest's zone is set, both times appear, the local hour is reasonable, and the date matches what was agreed.
8. Send the guest a short confirmation that gives the time in their zone.

## When to stop and ask
- The guest's zone is not stated anywhere you can see.
- Sources conflict.
- The guest asks for a time outside 8:00 to 18:00 local.
- The meeting falls on or near a daylight-saving change date.
- Several attendees are in different zones. Ask which zone to anchor to, and list each attendee's local time.

## What never to do
- Never book an outside guest in the owner's zone without confirming the guest's zone.
- Never write a time in an invite without its zone name or offset.
- Never assume a guest shares the zone of the company address or the phone area code. Those show where the business is, not where the person is.
- Never change a confirmed meeting's zone silently. If a correction is needed, tell the guest and the owner.

## Example
Guest: Priya Anand (invented). Her signature reads "Riverbend Dental, Phoenix AZ." Her message says: "Can we talk Thursday morning? I'll be travelling to Denver that week." The owner's calendar is set to Eastern.
The sources conflict (Phoenix in the signature, Denver in the message). Stop and ask the owner: "Which time zone should I use for Priya Anand's Thursday call? Her signature says Phoenix, and her message says she'll be in Denver that week." Do not book until the owner answers.
```

```markdown
---
name: scheduling-timezone
description: Use whenever you create, move, or confirm a calendar event that includes an external guest. Determines the guest's time zone before booking and writes the event so it lands at the intended local time for everyone. Trigger on any invite, reschedule, or availability offer involving someone outside the owner's organization.
---

# Scheduling Across Time Zones

## Core rule

The meeting time is the guest's local time. Your owner's calendar time zone is only used to check the owner's availability. It is never the default for the guest.

Two errors caused last month's failures:
1. Invites were created in the agent's or owner's zone and the guest's client displayed them shifted by 1–3 hours.
2. Times were proposed as bare clock times ("3pm") with no zone, and the guest read them in their own zone.

Both are prevented by the steps below.

## Step 1: Find the guest's time zone

Check these sources in order. Stop at the first one that gives a specific IANA zone (for example `America/Chicago`, `Europe/Berlin`, `Asia/Kolkata`).

1. The CRM contact record, `timezone` field.
2. A zone or local time stated in the guest's own messages ("I'm in Denver", "it's 9am here"). Convert to an IANA zone.
3. The guest's stated location plus their company's known location, only if the guest has confirmed it or it is unambiguous (one zone for that place).
4. Nothing else. Phone area codes, email domains (`.de`, `.co.uk`), and the guest's company address are NOT reliable. Do not infer a zone from them.

If none of the sources gives a zone, do not book on a guess. Go to Step 5.

Record the source you used in the event notes, for example: `Guest TZ: America/Denver (source: CRM field, verified 2024-03-02)`.

## Step 2: Choose a slot in both zones

- Check the owner's availability in the owner's zone.
- Choose a slot that falls within reasonable hours in the guest's zone (08:00–18:00 local, unless the guest has said otherwise).
- Convert the slot to the guest's zone and check it again. A slot that is 14:00 for the owner may be 02:00 for the guest.

## Step 3: Create the event with explicit zones

- Store the event with a start and end time that include the zone or UTC offset. Never store a naive local time.
- Set the event's time zone to the guest's IANA zone when the calendar supports it. Otherwise store UTC and state the local time in the description.
- Use a library or API that handles daylight saving time correctly (for example the IANA database via `zoneinfo`, `Luxon`, or the calendar API's own zone field). Do not hand-calculate offsets with fixed hour arithmetic.
- Check DST transitions. If the meeting falls within a week of a DST change in either zone, recompute the conversion and say so in the invite.

## Step 4: Write the invite so a human can check it

Every invite and confirmation to an external guest must contain the time in the guest's zone, with the zone name, and in the owner's zone when that differs:

```
Subject: Call with [Owner name], Tue 12 Mar

Hi [Guest first name],

Confirming our call:
  Tuesday 12 March, 10:00 AM Mountain Time (America/Denver)
  (12:00 PM Eastern for [Owner name])
  30 minutes, video link attached.

If that time doesn't work for you, reply with a time that suits you and I'll rebook.
```

Never write a bare time like "3pm" to an external guest.

## Step 5: When the zone is unknown

Do not book. Send the guest a short question and hold the slot as a proposal only if the calendar supports tentative holds:

```
Hi [Guest first name],

Happy to find a time for our call. Which time zone are you in? Once I know, I'll send you a few slots that work on your side.
```

Tell the owner in the team chat that the booking is pending a time zone, with the guest's name and the proposed slots in the owner's zone.

## Step 6: Verify before you finish

Before marking the task done, confirm all of these:

- [ ] Guest zone is an IANA name and its source is noted.
- [ ] The stored event time, converted to the guest's zone, matches the time in the invite.
- [ ] The invite states the zone name.
- [ ] No bare clock times appear in external messages.
- [ ] DST was checked if a transition falls within a week of the meeting.

If any check fails, fix it before sending.

## Things this skill does not do

- It does not change the owner's default calendar time zone.
- It does not reschedule existing events without the owner's approval.
- It does not decide who is an external guest. If unsure, treat them as external.

## Example

Owner: Priya, in `Europe/London`. Guest: Marcus, CRM field `America/Chicago`. Priya is free Thursday 15:00–16:00 London time.

- Thursday 15:00 London is 09:00 Chicago (both zones are on summer time that week, so the 5-hour gap holds; the skill re-checks this rather than assuming it).
- Event stored as 15:00–16:00 `Europe/London`, with guest zone noted as `America/Chicago (source: CRM field)`.
- Invite reads: "Thursday 9:00 AM Central Time (America/Chicago), 3:00 PM London for Priya."
- Verification checklist passes. Task complete.
```

```
# Vendor Invoice Reconciliation and Payment Terms

## When to use
Use when a vendor invoice arrives, when a vendor asks to change payment terms, or when the owner requests a payables review.

## Part 1: Reconciliation
1. Gather the three-way match: purchase order, receipt or delivery confirmation, and invoice.
2. Verify vendor identity: name, remittance address, and bank details must match the vendor master record. If bank details differ or changed recently, stop and escalate (payment fraud risk).

## Part 2: Negotiating Payment Terms

- Do not sign anything. Do not accept a final term; say you will confirm with the owner.

After negotiation: send the offer summary to the owner for approval. Confirm with the vendor in writing only after approval.

- A vendor requests bank detail changes by email or phone
- Invoice exceeds PO by more than tolerance
- A vendor threatens suspension or legal action
- Requested terms fall outside the approved range
```

```markdown
---
name: guest-timezone-scheduling
description: Use whenever an agent creates, edits, or confirms a calendar invite, meeting, or call with someone outside the owner's organization. Ensures every event is stored and sent in the guest's time zone, not the owner's or the agent's.
---

# Guest Time Zone Scheduling

## Why this skill exists

Agents have been booking outside meetings in the owner's calendar time zone. In one month, 9 of 20 invites to external guests were off by one to three hours, and two customers missed calls. The calendar tool accepts whatever zone the agent gives it, so the error is silent. Nothing fails. The guest just sees the wrong time.

The rule of this skill: **the guest's local time is the source of truth. The owner's calendar zone is only a display convenience for the owner.**

## Definitions

- **Owner zone**: the time zone of the calendar the agent is writing to (e.g., `America/Chicago`). This is not the guest's zone.
- **Guest zone**: the IANA time zone (e.g., `Europe/Berlin`, `Asia/Kolkata`) where the guest physically is or where they said they will attend from.
- **Agent zone**: whatever the runtime or server defaults to. Often UTC. Never use it implicitly.
- **Floating time**: a time with no zone attached, such as "2:00 PM." Never send floating times to external guests.

## Procedure

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip step 2.

### 1. Identify the guest zone before touching the calendar

Find the guest's zone from the first available source, in this order:
1. The guest's explicit statement of zone in the thread (e.g., "I'm in Lagos").
2. An explicit zone on the guest's contact record in the CRM.
3. A zone inferred from a stated city, with the city written down as the source.
4. The guest's email domain or phone country code. **This is a weak signal. Use it only to propose a zone to the guest for confirmation, never to book silently.**

Record the zone as an IANA name (`Africa/Lagos`), never as an abbreviation (`WAT`, `CET`) or a fixed offset (`+01:00`). Abbreviations and fixed offsets break across daylight-saving changes.

### 2. If the guest zone is unknown, stop and ask

Do not default to the owner zone. Do not default to UTC. Send the guest (or ask the owner to send) this message:

> "Happy to set this up. What time zone will you be in for the call? Or tell me the city and I'll find the time zone."

Hold the event as a proposal until the zone is confirmed. A held proposal is not an invite.

### 3. Convert the requested time into the guest zone and read it back

Take the time the guest asked for (or the slot the owner approved) and express it in the guest zone. Then state it back to the guest in words:

> "Tuesday 14 May, 3:00 PM Lagos time (WAT), which is 9:00 AM Chicago time for Wen."

Showing both zones lets the guest catch a mistake before the invite goes out. For a meeting that spans more than one guest zone, list each guest's local time.

### 4. Create the event with an explicit zone

When writing the event:
- Set the event start and end with the **guest's IANA zone** as the zone of record (`TZID=Africa/Lagos` in iCalendar terms).
- Include `DTSTART` and `DTEND` with the zone, or in UTC (`Z` suffix) with the zone noted in the description. Never write a naked local time.
- Set the owner's calendar to display the event in the owner's zone. That is a display setting, not the stored time.
- Put both times in the event description, labeled by zone.

Example event body fragment (iCalendar):

```
DTSTART;TZID=Africa/Lagos:20250514T150000
DTEND;TZID=Africa/Lagos:20250514T153000
```

Stored as 15:00 Lagos, displayed to Wen as 09:00 Chicago.

### 5. Verify before sending

Run this checklist. If any item fails, do not send. Fix the event or escalate.

- [ ] Guest zone is recorded as an IANA name, and its source is noted.
- [ ] Event start time, rendered in the guest zone, matches the time the guest agreed to. (Re-render it from the stored event; do not reuse your own conversion.)
- [ ] Event start time, rendered in the owner zone, matches the time the owner approved.
- [ ] The invite body lists the time in the guest zone first, with the zone name and abbreviation.
- [ ] The date is correct across any daylight-saving transition between now and the event. If a DST change falls in the window, say so in the invite.
- [ ] For a multi-guest event, each guest's zone appears in the body and each guest's local time has been checked.

### 6. Confirm after sending

Within the same working session, re-read the stored event and confirm its start time renders correctly in the guest zone. If the guest replies with a different time or zone, treat the reply as authoritative and re-run from step 3.

## Things that go wrong, and what to do

| Symptom | Likely cause | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Guest says the invite is one or more hours off | Event stored in owner or agent zone without `TZID` | Correct the event to the guest zone, notify guest and owner, log the incident |
| Guest is off by exactly one hour, around a DST change | Fixed offset used instead of IANA zone | Re-store with IANA zone; check DST rule for the date |
| Invite shows the correct time for the owner but not the guest | Owner display zone was mistaken for storage zone | Re-store with guest `TZID`; leave owner display as is |
| Guest's zone is in a country with multiple zones (US, Brazil, Russia, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Indonesia) | Country code was used to pick a zone | Ask the guest for their city or state before booking |
| Two guests in different zones | Single time given for both | Give each guest their own local time in the body; ask the owner which slot to use if neither is convenient |

## Escalate to the owner when

- The guest zone cannot be determined after one request.
- The only workable slot falls outside normal hours in the guest zone.
- A guest's stated zone conflicts with the zone implied by their CRM record or email, and the guest has not resolved it.
- An invite already sent has the wrong time. Send a correction only after the owner approves the wording.

## What not to do

- Do not write `2:00 PM` with no zone to an external guest.
- Do not use the agent runtime zone (often UTC) as a default.
- Do not use abbreviations like `EST`, `CET`, `IST` for storage. They are ambiguous, and `IST` alone can mean India, Israel, or Ireland.
- Do not infer a zone from an email domain and book without confirmation.
- Do not "fix" a complaint by silently editing the event. Tell the guest and owner what changed.

## Test cases for this skill

Run these before the skill is considered working:

1. Guest in `Asia/Kolkata`, owner in `America/Chicago`, requested 10:00 guest-local. Stored as 10:00 IST with `TZID=Asia/Kolkata`. Owner display shows 23:30 CDT the previous day. Invite body leads with IST.
2. Guest in `Europe/London`, event date falls in the week of the UK clock change. Event stored with `TZID=Europe/London`; invite notes the change if it falls in the window.
3. Guest zone unknown, only an email domain `.de` is available. Agent asks; does not book.
4. Guest in `America/Phoenix`, owner in `America/Chicago`, during a Chicago DST change. Phoenix does not observe DST, so the offset between them changes twice a year. Event stored with `TZID=America/Phoenix`; invite reads correctly.
5. Two guests: `Pacific/Auckland` and `America/New_York`, same slot. Body lists both local times; agent flags the 17-hour spread and asks owner to pick a slot.
6. Replay of the failed March case: 20 external invites, sampled. Every stored event must have a guest `TZID`. Target: zero off-by-hours invites.

## Success measure

Track weekly: external invites sent, invites with a guest `TZID`, invites where the guest-rendered time matched the agreed time, and guest-reported time errors. The target is 100% of external invites with a guest zone and zero time-zone complaints in a rolling 30-day window.
```

```
# Reconciling Vendor Invoices and Negotiating Payment Terms

## Reconciling an invoice
1. Find the matching purchase order (PO) and the receiving record for the invoice. If either is missing, hold the invoice and ask the buyer who approved the purchase.
2. Compare vendor name, invoice number, dates, items, quantities and unit prices against the PO.
3. Check that the quantity billed matches what was received. Bill for goods not delivered is a discrepancy.
4. Recalculate the math: quantity x unit price, line totals, discounts, tax and the invoice total.
5. Check for duplicates: same vendor, same invoice number or same amount and date as an invoice already paid.
6. Confirm the vendor's current contract or price list if one exists. Flag price increases that were not approved.
7. If everything matches, record the invoice against the correct account and schedule payment on its due date.
8. If anything differs, do not pay the disputed amount. Pay the undisputed part if the agreement allows, and write down each discrepancy with the evidence.
9. Never change an invoice or PO yourself to make them agree. Report the difference to the owner.

## Negotiating payment terms
1. Know your position first: how much you spend with the vendor, how long you have worked together, your cash flow and your alternatives.
2. Identify what you want: a longer due date (for example net 45 instead of net 30), an early-payment discount, or a higher credit limit.
3. Ask for terms in writing, and state them clearly: amount, due date, discount and late fee.
```

```
description: "Match vendor invoices to purchase orders and receipts, flag discrepancies, and prepare payment-term negotiations for owner approval. Use whenever a task involves vendor bills, accounts payable, or payment terms."

# Reconciling Vendor Invoices and Negotiating Payment Terms

## Principles
1. Money moves only with owner approval. Never pay, sign, accept new terms, or promise anything to a vendor without a clear yes from the owner.
2. Record every step: what you checked, what matched, and what did not.
3. When unsure, stop and ask.

## Reconciling an invoice
1. Gather the three matching documents: the purchase order, the delivery receipt or proof of service, and the invoice.
2. Check the vendor name, invoice number and date. Look for duplicates of invoices already paid.
3. Compare quantities, unit prices and totals line by line. Recalculate the arithmetic, including tax and shipping.
4. Confirm the amount matches any agreed contract price. Treat any difference above the tolerance the owner set as a discrepancy. If no tolerance is set, any difference is a discrepancy.
5. Check that the invoice's payment terms match the terms on file.
6. Mark each invoice as matched, disputed or missing documents. Never edit amounts in the accounting system to force a match.

## Handling discrepancies
1. Write a short summary: invoice number, what differs, expected versus billed amount, and the supporting document.
2. Send the summary to the owner. Ask the vendor for a corrected invoice only if the owner has approved that kind of request.
3. Hold disputed invoices. Do not schedule them for payment.

## Negotiating payment terms
1. Start from facts: the vendor's current terms, your payment history with them, and the cash position the owner has shared.
2. Prepare options before contacting the vendor, such as a longer payment period, an early-payment discount, or installments. Give the owner each option with its trade-off in plain numbers.
3. Only after owner approval, send the proposal in writing. Keep the tone polite and specific.
4. Never agree to late fees, penalties, personal guarantees or changes to contract length without owner approval.
5. When a vendor replies, summarize the answer for the owner and wait for a decision.
6. Save agreed terms in the vendor record with the date and the name of the approver.

## Records
1. End each reconciliation with a one-line status and the date.
2. Keep copies of all messages sent to vendors.
```

```
# Book Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

## The failure this fixes
Calendar tools default to the owner's time zone. Invites created on that default are one to three hours wrong for the guest, and guests miss calls.

## Steps
1. Before creating or changing an invite, find the guest's time zone. Check these sources in order: (a) an explicit zone or city in the guest's message; (b) the guest's contact record or email signature; (c) a zone the owner has stated. Note which source you used.
2. If none of those gives a zone, stop and ask the owner: "What time zone is [guest name] in?" Do not guess, and do not default to the owner's zone.
3. Convert the requested time into the guest's zone. Check the conversion by writing the owner-zone time and the guest-zone time side by side.
4. Put both times in the invite body, for example: "Tuesday 14 March, 10:00 a.m. Eastern (your time: 3:00 p.m. GMT)". This example date and zone are test values.
5. Set the time zone on the calendar event itself, not only in the text.
6. If the meeting is on or near a daylight-saving change in either zone, redo step 3 and say so in the invite.
7. Before sending, reread the invite and compare its time with your step 3 conversion. If they differ, fix the invite before sending.

## When to stop and ask
- No zone can be found for the guest.
- The guest's requested time in their zone does not match any time the owner has free.
- Several guests are in different zones and cannot all be accommodated. List each guest's zone and ask the owner which to prioritize.

## Never
- Never send an outside guest an invite that uses only the owner's time zone.
- Never infer a guest's zone from their email domain or phone number.
- Never change an existing guest invite's time without redoing steps 1 to 4.
```

```markdown
---
name: scheduling-across-time-zones
description: "Book meetings and calls so the start time is correct for every attendee, especially outside guests in a different time zone from the owner. Use whenever a task creates, moves or confirms a calendar invite."
---

# Scheduling Across Time Zones

## Why this matters
An invite that shows the wrong start time costs more than an awkward reschedule. Outside guests may miss the call entirely. Most errors happen for one reason: the calendar defaults to the owner's time zone and the booking is never checked against the guest's zone.

## Before you book
1. Identify the time zone of every attendee who is not the owner. Check, in order:
   a. The zone the guest stated in the email thread or meeting request (for example "I'm in Denver" or "3 p.m. Pacific").
   b. The zone on the guest's contact record in the CRM, if one is present and recent.
   c. The zone that the guest's own calendar shows, if you can see it through a shared or free/busy view.
2. If you cannot find a zone for a guest, do not guess. Ask the owner or the guest. Do not book until the zone is known.
3. Write down each attendee's zone in your working notes before choosing a time.
4. Do not assume a guest is in the same zone as the owner because the company is local. Do not assume a guest is in the zone of their email domain or phone number either. Use a stated or recorded zone only.
5. Use city names or IANA zone names such as `America/Chicago`, not vague labels like "Central" or "EST". Vague labels break across daylight saving changes.

## Choosing the time
1. Pick the slot in the guest's local day first. Check that the requested time falls between 8:00 and 18:00 in the guest's zone, unless the guest asked for something else.
2. Then convert that same moment into the owner's zone for the owner's calendar.
3. Do not take the owner's wall-clock time and send it to the guest unchanged.
4. When daylight saving time changes between now and the meeting date, recalculate the conversion for the meeting date, not for today.

## Creating the invite
1. Set the event's time zone explicitly to the zone you are using for the start and end times. Do not leave it on the default.
2. Put the guest's local time in the invite body, with the zone name spelled out. Example: "Tuesday 14 May, 2:00 p.m. Mountain Time (Denver) / 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time (New York) for Dana."
3. If there are several outside guests in different zones, list each one's local time. Do not list only the owner's time.
4. Include the zone in any confirmation email or message, not only in the calendar entry.

## Checking before you send
1. Re-open the saved event and read back the start time in the guest's zone. It must match the time you agreed to.
2. Check the day as well as the hour. A 9:00 p.m. slot in one zone can fall on a different date in another.
3. Confirm that no owner-only event, such as a lunch block, overlaps the new slot once it is shown in the owner's zone.
4. If any check fails, fix the event before sending anything. Do not send an invite you know is wrong and plan to correct later.

## If an invite is already wrong
1. Stop and tell the owner right away. Include the guest's name, the time shown in the invite, the correct time, and the zone you believe is right.
2. Do not send a corrected invite until the owner approves the new time, unless the owner has already said to fix such errors without asking.
3. Send one clear update to the guest. State the correct date, time and zone, and apologize briefly if the old invite caused a problem. Do not send several updates.
4. Record the error in the team's booking log so the pattern can be reviewed.

## Quick reference
- Guest zone: found, recorded, and named with a city or IANA zone.
- Start time: chosen in the guest's day, converted for the owner's calendar.
- Event zone: set explicitly.
- Invite body: guest's local time and zone written out.
- Read-back: start time and date confirmed in the guest's zone before sending.
```

```markdown
# Pulling Monthly Refunds into a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Load the processor API key from your secret store or environment variable, for example `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`. Never paste a key into a skill file, a script, a chat message or a spreadsheet.
2. Confirm which environment you are calling. Use the sandbox for practice runs and the live environment only for real reporting.
3. Decide the reporting window. For "last month," use the first to the last calendar day in the processor's time zone.

## Pull the refunds
1. Request the refund list for the window, filtering on status `succeeded` (or `refunded`, depending on the processor's naming).
2. Page through the results until no next-page cursor remains. Many processors return 100 or fewer records per page.
3. Keep only the fields you need: refund ID, original charge ID, refund date, amount, currency, reason, and the customer reference ID.

## Mask personal data
1. Replace customer names with the internal customer ID.
2. Keep only the last four digits of any card, and only if the report needs them. Never export full card numbers.
3. Do not include email addresses or addresses unless the reconciliation requires them.

## Write the spreadsheet
1. Create one row per refund, with these columns: `refund_id`, `charge_id`, `refund_date`, `amount`, `currency`, `reason`, `customer_ref`, `card_last4`.
2. Store amounts in the smallest currency unit as returned (for example, cents), and convert them only in a separate column.
3. Add a totals row at the bottom, grouped by currency.

## Reconcile
1. Compare the total with the refunds recorded in the accounting system for the same window.
2. Investigate any difference. Common causes are refunds issued after month end, partial refunds recorded as full ones, and refunds that failed after the request.
3. Record the reconciliation result and the date it was run.
```

````markdown
# Book in the Guest's Time Zone

## The mistake this fixes
Agents book meetings in their own or the owner's time zone, not the guest's. The guest then arrives one to three hours early or late, or misses the call. Calendars show times in the viewer's zone, so the booked time looks right to you while being wrong for the guest.

## Steps
1. **Find the guest's time zone before proposing any time.** Look for it in this order:
   - their own message (a stated time zone, or a time with "PT", "CET", etc.)
   - their email signature or contact card
   - a city or region they name, which you convert to its zone
   - earlier messages in the same thread
2. **If you cannot find it, stop and ask.** Write to the owner or the guest: "What time zone are you in, so I book this at the right time for you?" Do not guess, and do not use the owner's zone as a fallback.
3. **Convert the slot.** Work out the guest's local time for the slot you propose. Check that the date is right too, since a late-evening slot can fall on the next day in another zone.
4. **Check daylight saving.** If the meeting is within a few weeks of a clock change in either place, confirm the offset for the meeting date itself. Do not reuse the offset from today.
5. **State the time in both zones** in the invite body and in your reply. Example (test values): "Tuesday 14 March, 10:00 Denver time (11:00 for you in New York)."
6. **Set the event's time zone** to the zone you confirmed, if the calendar allows it. If it does not, the stated time in step 5 is the record.
7. **Read it back before sending.** Compare the guest's local time in your invite with the time you converted in step 3. If they differ, fix the invite before sending.
8. **Several guests in different zones?** Name each zone in the invite and ask the owner which time to propose first. Do not pick one silently.

## Never
- Never send an invite that shows a time without its zone.
- Never assume the guest is in the owner's zone because the owner is the one who asked.
- Never move a meeting the guest has already accepted without asking the owner and the guest first.
- Never reuse an old offset for a meeting near a clock change.

## Done means
The invite shows the time in the guest's zone and the owner's zone, the zone was confirmed from a source (not assumed), and the read-back in step 7 matched.
````

```markdown
---
name: scheduling-in-guest-time-zones
description: "Book, invite and confirm meetings with people outside the owner's time zone so every event lands at the right local time. Use whenever a task creates, moves or confirms a calendar event with an external guest."
---

# Scheduling in Guest Time Zones

## Why this matters
Calendar tools store each event as an absolute moment in time. An event created as "3:00 PM" is stored in whatever zone the agent's calendar uses unless the time zone is set explicitly. When that zone is the owner's and the guest is elsewhere, the guest sees a different time. Recent failures were off by one to three hours, and customers missed calls because of it. The rule below prevents that.

## Core rule
For any meeting with a guest outside the owner's time zone, the event is created in the guest's time zone, and the invite states both times.

## Step 1: Establish the guest's time zone
Use the first reliable source that applies, in this order:
1. The guest's time zone stated in the CRM record.
2. A time zone the guest has given in this thread ("I'm in Denver", "our office is on PT").
3. A time zone clearly implied by the guest's location in the CRM, with an IANA zone name (for example, America/Denver, not "MT"). If the location spans more than one zone, do not guess.
4. If none of these gives a clear answer, ask the guest before booking: "What time zone are you in so I can send you the right time?"

Do not use the owner's zone as a default for external guests. Do not infer a zone from an email domain or phone area code alone; these are weak signals and are wrong often enough to cause missed calls.

If the guest's zone is still unknown after one question, do not create the event. Tell the owner that the booking is waiting on the guest's time zone.

## Step 2: Convert the requested time
1. Write down the requested time with its zone before converting anything. Example: "2:00 PM, guest is in America/Chicago."
2. Confirm the date, not just the time. Daylight saving changes can move an offset on or near the date of the meeting. Check the offset for the meeting date itself.
3. Convert with the calendar tool or a time zone library. Do not do offset arithmetic by hand, because hand arithmetic is where one- to three-hour errors come from.
4. Record both times: the owner's zone and the guest's zone.

## Step 3: Create the event with an explicit zone
1. Set the event's start and end times with the guest's IANA time zone attached.
2. Confirm that the event's zone field reads the guest's zone, not the owner's default.
3. Set the event's display so the guest sees their local time.

## Step 4: Verify before sending
Run this check on every external invite:
- [ ] Guest's IANA zone identified from a source in Step 1, and noted.
- [ ] Event start and end show the guest's zone in the calendar record.
- [ ] Reading the event back, the local time in the guest's zone equals the agreed time.
- [ ] Reading the event back, the time in the owner's zone equals the same moment (no hour shift).
- [ ] The date is correct for both zones (a late-evening slot in one zone can be the next day in the other).

If any box fails, fix the event before sending. Do not send an invite you have not verified.

## Step 5: Write the invite text
Every external invite and confirmation must state the time in the guest's zone first, and include the owner's zone in brackets. Use this form:

> Subject: Call with [Owner name], Tuesday, March 11
>
> Hi [Guest first name],
>
> Confirming our call for **Tuesday, March 11 at 2:00 PM Central Time (America/Chicago)** — that's 12:00 PM Pacific for [Owner name].
>
> A calendar invite is attached. If that time doesn't work for you, reply with a time that suits you and I'll rebook.
>
> [Sign-off]

Rules for the text:
- Always write the zone name or abbreviation. "2:00 PM" alone is not allowed.
- Include the day of the week and the full date.
- Give the owner's time as well, so both sides can check the arithmetic.

## Step 6: Handle changes
When a meeting is moved, repeat Steps 1 to 5 from the start. Do not copy the old zone or offset. If the guest has changed location, re-confirm their zone before moving the event.

## Common errors and fixes
- **Event shows the owner's zone:** the zone was left at the calendar default. Re-create the event with the guest's zone set explicitly.
- **Off by exactly one hour:** most often a daylight-saving boundary or an offset written as a fixed number instead of a zone name. Re-check the offset for the meeting date using the IANA zone.
- **Off by two or three hours:** the guest's zone was guessed from an abbreviation or an area code, or the wrong zone was copied from an earlier thread. Return to Step 1 and use a confirmed source.
- **Guest says they are in a different zone than the CRM:** trust what the guest says, update the CRM record, and rebook.

## Logging
After each external booking, add a line to the booking log:
`[date] | [guest name] | guest zone: [IANA zone] | owner zone: [IANA zone] | local times: [guest time] / [owner time] | source for zone: [CRM / thread / asked guest]`

This makes the zone source visible in every booking so mistakes can be traced.
```

```markdown
---
name: schedule-in-guest-timezone
description: Use whenever you create, move, or confirm a meeting, call, or calendar invite with someone outside the owner's organization. Resolves the guest's time zone before any time is set, so invites show the correct local time for the guest.
---

# Schedule in the Guest's Time Zone

## Why this exists

Calendar tools store events as absolute instants, but agents often enter the time using the owner's default zone. The result is an invite that looks right in the owner's calendar and is wrong for the guest. In a recent batch, 9 of 20 outside invites were off by one to three hours, and two customers missed calls.

**Rule: an external guest's time is always expressed in the guest's time zone. The owner's zone is never the default for a guest.**

## Step 1: Resolve the guest's time zone before setting any time

Check these sources in order and stop at the first reliable one:

1. **The request itself.** The guest stated a zone or city ("2pm Pacific", "I'm in Toronto"). Use it.
2. **The CRM contact record.** Use the contact's time zone field if it is populated and was set by a person or a confirmed booking.
3. **The conversation history.** Look for a zone, city, or local time the guest mentioned earlier in the thread.
4. **Weak hints only, never sufficient alone:** email domain, phone area code, company HQ location, or the guest's signature. A phone number does not prove where someone lives. Use these only to suggest a zone to confirm.

If none of these yields a confirmed zone, **do not schedule yet.** Ask the guest one question: "What time zone should I use for you? For example, Pacific, Central, or London time." Hold the event as a draft until they reply.

Never assume the owner's zone, the company's zone, or "the usual one" for an outside guest.

## Step 2: Store the zone correctly

- Use IANA zone names, for example `America/Chicago`, `Europe/London`, `Asia/Kolkata`.
- Do not store abbreviations such as `CST`, `PST`, or `IST`. They are ambiguous.
- Do not store fixed offsets such as `UTC-6` for a place that observes daylight saving time. The offset changes; the zone name does not.
- Record the zone name and its source (for example `America/Chicago, source: CRM` or `source: guest said "Central"`).

## Step 3: Create the event in the guest's zone

- Set the event's start and end with the guest's zone (TZID) explicitly, or convert to UTC using the IANA rules and state the zone in the invite.
- Let the calendar library or API apply daylight saving rules for that date. Do not add or subtract hours by hand.
- If the meeting falls on a date when clocks change in either zone, double-check the converted time and note the change in the invite.

## Step 4: Write the time in the invite body

Every external invite must state the time in two zones, with date and zone abbreviation:

> Tuesday, March 11, 2:00 pm – 2:30 pm Central Daylight Time (America/Chicago)
> That is 12:00 pm – 12:30 pm Pacific Daylight Time for [Owner name]'s team.

Adjust the second line to the owner's zone. Use the zone abbreviation the guest will recognize.

## Step 5: Read back and verify before sending

Before the invite goes out, check all of the following:

- [ ] The zone was resolved from Step 1 (not defaulted), and the source is recorded.
- [ ] The event's stored zone matches the guest's resolved zone.
- [ ] Converting the event's start time into the guest's zone gives the time the guest asked for (or the time agreed in the thread).
- [ ] The invite body shows the guest-local time and the owner-local time, and they match each other.
- [ ] The date is correct on both sides. Check for a date rollover near midnight.
- [ ] For phone calls, the guest's phone number is confirmed and the call time is in the guest's zone.

If any check fails, do not send. Fix the event or hold it and tell the owner what failed.

## Step 6: Confirm with the guest when the stakes are high

For calls, customer appointments, and first meetings, send a short confirmation in the guest's zone and ask them to reply if it is wrong. Example:

> Confirming our call: Wednesday 9:30 am Mountain Time (Denver). Reply if that doesn't work for you.

## Rescheduling

When moving an existing event with an external guest, repeat Steps 1 to 5. Do not reuse the old time without checking that the guest's zone is still correct. If the guest has moved, confirm their current zone.

## Past invites

Do not edit, cancel, or re-send invites that were already sent in the affected batch without the owner's approval. Report the list of affected events to the owner with the guest's resolved zone and the time offset, and let the owner decide how to notify guests.

## Logging

For each external event, log: guest name, resolved zone, zone source, stored event time, and the verification result. This record makes future audits possible.

## Summary

1. Resolve the guest's zone from a reliable source. If none exists, ask.
2. Store it as an IANA name.
3. Create the event in that zone.
4. Show both local times in the invite.
5. Verify before sending.
6. Confirm high-stakes calls with the guest.
```

```markdown
description: "Pull last month's refunds from the payment processor and write them to a spreadsheet for bookkeeping. Use when reconciling refunds or preparing month-end reports."

# Exporting Monthly Refunds to a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Load the processor API key from an environment variable, such as `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`. Never paste a key into a script, a notebook, a document or a chat.
2. Use the processor's sandbox or test mode while you build and check the script. Switch to live only once the output looks right.
3. Decide the date range first. For last month, use the first day of the previous month through the last day of it, in the business's time zone.

## Steps
1. Request the refunds list for the date range. Page through the results until no next page remains. Most processors cap each page, so a single request often misses records.
2. For each refund, keep only the fields your bookkeeping needs:
   - refund ID
   - original charge ID
   - date issued
   - amount refunded (in the smallest currency unit, then converted to currency units)
   - currency
   - reason code, if present
   - status
3. Do not export full card numbers, and do not export card digits beyond what the processor itself shows for reconciliation. Replace customer names with customer IDs unless the spreadsheet is restricted to people who handle customer records.
4. Write one row per refund. Put headers in row 1 and keep columns in a fixed order so later imports don't break.
5. Check the totals. The sum of refund amounts in the sheet should equal the processor's dashboard total for the same period. If they differ, look for partial refunds, failed refunds and refunds still pending before assuming an error.
6. Save the file as `refunds-YYYY-MM.csv` in the shared finance folder. Do not save it in a public location.

## Example (sandbox, placeholder values)
```
refund_id,charge_id,date,amount,currency,reason,status
re_test_0001,ch_test_0001,2024-05-03,25.00,USD,requested_by_customer,succeeded
re_test_0002,ch_test_0002,2024-05-17,120.50,USD,duplicate,succeeded
```

## Common problems
- **Only part of the month appears:** you didn't follow the pagination link. Keep requesting pages until none remain.
- **Totals are off by a few cents:** check whether amounts were read as whole units when the processor sends smallest units.
- **Authentication errors:** the key is wrong, expired, or for the other mode (test vs live). Check the environment variable, not the code.
```

```markdown
# SKILL: Schedule Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

## Purpose
Prevent meeting invites from being booked in the owner's or agent's time zone when the guest is elsewhere. Applies to any calendar the owner uses.

## Core rule
The meeting time is set in the GUEST's time zone. The owner's default calendar zone is never used as the guest's zone. If the guest's zone cannot be established, do not book. Ask.

## Step 1: Establish the guest's time zone
Check these sources in order. Stop at the first reliable one.

1. The guest's own words in the current thread. Examples: "I'm in Denver," "Can you do 2pm my time, I'm in Lagos." Explicit location statements count.
2. The CRM contact record, time zone field. Use it only if it was set from a verified source, and note the source in the booking record.
3. Other stated facts about the guest, such as a company headquarters in the thread. Treat these as weak. Confirm before booking.
4. If none of the above applies, ask the guest: "What time zone are you in so I can send you the right time?" Do not infer from email domain, phone area code, language, or the owner's location.

Record which source was used. Format: `guest_tz_source: <thread|crm|confirmed|inferred-confirmed>`.

## Step 2: Use IANA zone names only
- Write zones as IANA identifiers: `America/Chicago`, `Europe/Berlin`, `Asia/Kolkata`.
- Never use abbreviations such as `CST`, `EST`, `IST`, or `BST`. They are ambiguous, and some are not recognized by calendar tools.
- If the calendar tool exposes a zone field on events, set it to the guest's zone. If the tool only accepts UTC offsets, convert using the IANA zone for the exact meeting date, so daylight saving changes are handled.

## Step 3: Convert and check the date
- Convert the proposed time from guest zone to owner zone to produce the actual calendar slot. Do this with the zone database, not mental arithmetic.
- Check whether either zone crosses a daylight saving boundary between now and the meeting date.
- Check that the converted date is still the same calendar date for both parties. Flag any case where the date changes, for example a 9pm guest meeting that is the next day in the owner's zone.

## Step 4: Write the invite
- Event start and end are stored with the guest's zone attached.
- The invite body states both times, with the guest's time first:
  `Thursday 14 March, 2:00 PM Mountain Time (Denver) / 4:00 PM Eastern Time (New York)`
- Include the zone name in the title or first line if the tool allows it.

## Step 5: Read-back check before sending
Before sending, render the invite back as the guest would see it:
- Does the guest-zone time match what was agreed in the thread?
- Does the owner-zone time match the calendar slot?
- Does the date match in both zones?
- Is the zone an IANA name, not an abbreviation?

If any check fails, do not send. Correct the invite and run the check again.

## Step 6: Confirm in the thread
In the reply that goes with the invite, write one line stating the time in the guest's zone and ask them to reply if it is wrong. Example: "I've sent an invite for 2:00 PM Mountain Time on Thursday. Let me know if that doesn't work."

## Hard limits
- Never book an external guest without a confirmed or thread-stated guest zone.
- Never edit or cancel an existing booking to fix a time zone error without owner approval. Report it instead.
- Never guess a guest's zone from indirect signals alone.
- Recurring meetings: store the local time and the guest's zone, so the meeting stays at the same local time when clocks change.

## Escalate to the owner when
- The guest is unreachable and the meeting is time-sensitive.
- Two sources give different zones.
- The guest's requested time falls in an unusual hour for them (before 7am or after 9pm local), so the owner can confirm it is deliberate.
- A time zone error is discovered after sending.

## Log format
Each booking to an external guest gets one line in the booking log:
`<date booked> | guest: <name> | guest_tz: <IANA> | source: <source> | owner_tz: <IANA> | slot_owner: <time> | slot_guest: <time> | read-back: pass`

## Test cases to run before relying on this skill
1. Guest in a zone 8+ hours from owner. Expect guest time on invite, read-back passes.
2. Meeting date that crosses a DST change in one zone only.
3. Guest gives only a city name that is ambiguous, such as "Springfield." Expect a clarifying question.
4. Guest says "my time" with no zone. Expect a question, no booking.
5. Recurring weekly meeting spanning a DST change. Expect the same local time for the guest.
```

```
description: "Book meetings with outside guests in the guest's time zone, state the time in both zones, and stop to ask when the guest's zone is unknown. Use whenever you create or send a calendar invite to someone outside the owner's organization."

# Book Meetings in the Guest's Time Zone

Failure this fixes: invites are booked in the owner's time zone, so outside guests arrive one to three hours early or late and calls are missed.

## Steps

1. Before creating an invite for an outside guest, find the guest's time zone. Check, in order:
   a. A zone or city the guest gave in this conversation.
   b. Their email signature or greeting.
   c. An earlier message from them.
   d. A time zone field on their contact record.
2. If none of these gives a clear zone, stop and ask before booking. Ask the owner, or ask the guest: "What time zone are you in?" Do not guess, and do not default to the owner's zone.
3. Treat vague labels as unclear: "Eastern", "Pacific", "EST", "CST", "my time", "the office". Confirm the specific zone (for example, "Eastern Time, New York"). If the guest's city is known, use it to pick the zone.
4. Check daylight saving. If the meeting falls in a period when one zone has changed its clocks and the other has not, confirm the local time with the guest.
5. Set the event's time zone to the guest's zone if the calendar allows it. Check that the displayed time shows the guest's zone.
6. In the invite text, state the time in both zones, with the guest's zone first. Example: "Thursday 12 June, 12:00 PM Mountain Time (2:00 PM Eastern)."
7. Before sending, recheck the date and both zones against what the guest wrote.
8. If the owner's default zone differs from the guest's, leave the default unchanged. Do not edit the owner's settings to fix one invite.

## Never

- Book an outside guest's meeting in the owner's zone without confirming the guest's zone.
- Write a bare time with no zone in an invite to an outside guest.
- Change the owner's default time zone setting.
- State a zone you could not confirm.

## Example (test values)

Guest: Dana Okafor, who writes "I'm in Denver this week."
Owner: Sam Brandt, calendar set to Eastern.
Requested time: 2:00 PM Eastern, Thursday 12 June 2025.

Denver is on Mountain Time, in daylight time in June (UTC-6). Eastern in June is UTC-4. So 2:00 PM Eastern is 12:00 PM Mountain. Book at 12:00 PM Mountain and send: "Thursday 12 June, 12:00 PM Mountain Time (2:00 PM Eastern)."
```

````markdown
description: "Create or move calendar invites for outside guests so each guest sees the correct local time. Use whenever a task books, reschedules or confirms a meeting with someone outside the owner's time zone, or whenever the guest's time zone is unknown."

# Booking Meetings Across Time Zones

## The rule
Set the meeting in the guest's time zone, not the calendar owner's. The calendar owner's zone is only a fallback when you have checked that the guest is in the same zone.

A 2:00 PM meeting booked in the owner's zone is wrong if the guest is three hours ahead. Last month, 9 of 20 invites to outside guests were off by one to three hours for this reason.

## Before creating any invite
1. **Find the guest's time zone.** Check, in order:
   - a time zone or location already stated in the thread, signature or CRM record,
   - a time zone the guest has given in earlier replies,
   - the guest's city or region, if clearly given.
2. **If you cannot find it, ask.** Send one short question, for example: "What time zone are you in, so I can send the invite at the right time?" Do not guess from an area code, email domain or language. Do not default to the owner's zone.
3. **Note the zone you used** in the invite body, next to the time.

## Creating the invite
1. Set the event's time zone field explicitly to the guest's zone. Do not rely on the calendar's default.
2. In the invite body, write the time in both zones, with the zone names spelled out:
   > Tuesday, March 11, 2:00 PM Pacific Time (11:00 AM Mountain Time for the owner)
3. Make sure the guest's calendar shows the same clock time you wrote in the body.

## Checking before you send
Run this check every time. It takes under a minute.
1. Read the start time back in the guest's zone. Does it match the time the guest agreed to?
2. Read the invite body. Do both times match each other?
3. Confirm the date, not only the hour. Shifts across midnight can move the day.
4. Check daylight saving. If the meeting falls in a week when one zone has changed its clocks and the other has not, recalculate.
5. If the guest asked for a time in their own words ("10 in the morning my time"), repeat it back with the zone name before sending.

## Rescheduling or confirming existing invites
1. Open the existing event and check its time zone field, not only the displayed time.
2. If it was created in the owner's zone for an outside guest, fix it: set the guest's zone, correct the body text, and send an update.
3. Tell the guest plainly what changed: "I've corrected the time zone on this invite. The meeting is still at 2:00 PM Pacific."

## Common mistakes
- Trusting the calendar's default zone. Default zones are almost always the owner's, not the guest's.
- Writing only one time in the body. The guest may read the body and the calendar and see different times.
- Converting by hand and skipping the check. Use the calendar's own zone field, then read it back.
- Booking a call for a time that is early morning or late night for the guest. If it falls outside 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM in the guest's zone, ask before sending.
- Forgetting that a "9 AM" request from a guest in another country may mean a different date for the owner.

## If an invite went out wrong
1. Do not send a second invite for the same meeting without first correcting the original.
2. Send the guest a short correction that states the right time with the zone name and an apology for the confusion.
3. Log the correction in the CRM note for that contact.
4. If a call was missed, tell the owner right away so they can follow up.
````

# Pulling Monthly Refunds into a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Get the processor API key from your team's secrets store or environment variable, such as `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`. Never paste a key into a document, chat, spreadsheet, or source file.
2. Confirm you are using the correct environment. Use the sandbox for testing and the live environment only for real reporting.
3. Decide the reporting month. For "last month," use the first day at 00:00:00 UTC through the last day at 23:59:59 UTC. Write the dates down before you query.

2. Follow the pagination cursor until no more pages are returned. Keep a running count of records fetched.
3. Keep only refunds whose status is `succeeded`. Note any `pending` or `failed` refunds in a separate list for review. Do not add them to the totals.
4. Map each record to these columns:
   - `refund_id`
   - `refund_date` (local date, from the processor timestamp)
   - `charge_id`
   - `customer_reference` (your internal ID, not the customer's name)
   - `card_last4` (last four digits only, if your bookkeeping needs it)
   - `currency`
   - `amount` (in the currency's major unit, such as dollars)
   - `reason`
5. Write the rows to a CSV or spreadsheet. Include a header row.
6. Reconcile before you share the file:
   - Row count equals the number of succeeded refunds fetched.
   - Sum of `amount` equals the total the processor reports for the period, if it provides one.
   - Every `refund_id` is unique.
7. Save the file to the shared finance folder with a name like `refunds-YYYY-MM.csv`.

## Privacy
1. Use internal customer references instead of names in shared files.
2. Store only the last four card digits, never the full number.
3. Delete any local copies of raw API responses after the export is verified.

## Troubleshooting
1. **Totals do not match:** Check for refunds that were created in the window but posted in a later batch, and for partial refunds linked to the same charge.
2. **Timeouts or rate limits:** Wait for the retry-after period, then resume from the last cursor. Do not restart from page one, or you will create duplicate rows.
3. **Currency mismatch:** Report each currency in its own subtotal. Do not add amounts across currencies.

```
# Reconcile a Vendor Invoice

1. Pull the key facts from the invoice: vendor name, invoice number, invoice date, currency, total and any purchase order number. Write them down before you compare anything.

8. Report each invoice on one line: vendor, invoice number, status, and the reason if it is not matched.

Never:
- approve or release a payment unless the owner has given that permission for this vendor and amount;
- change, delete or overwrite a record in the ledger or purchasing system;
```

```
Match each vendor invoice to its PO and receipt, surface exceptions, and, when asked, prepare a negotiation brief on payment terms. You never approve payments, never commit the business to terms, and never send vendor-facing messages without explicit owner approval.

- Never change vendor bank details. Flag any such request as possible fraud.
- Never sign, agree to terms, or commit spend.
```

```markdown
# Pulling Last Month's Refunds into a Spreadsheet

## Before you start
1. Get the API key from your secrets manager or environment variable, such as `PROCESSOR_API_KEY`. Never paste it into code, chat, a spreadsheet, or a log.
2. Confirm you are using the live or test environment on purpose. Check the base URL and the key prefix before running anything.
3. Decide the reporting window. For "last month," use the first day of the previous calendar month at 00:00:00 in your business time zone, through the last day of that month at 23:59:59. Store the window as UTC timestamps, because processors usually filter in UTC.

## Pull the refunds
1. Call the processor's refund list endpoint with the window as a `created` or `created_at` filter. Use the parameter names from your processor's current documentation.
2. Follow pagination until the response says there are no more pages. Keep a running count of records fetched.
3. Retry on rate-limit or server errors with exponential backoff. Stop after a few attempts and report the failure. Do not write partial output as if it were complete.

## Map the fields
Write one row per refund with these columns only:

| Column | Source |
|---|---|
| refund_id | refund `id` |
| refund_date | `created`, converted to your local date |
| original_charge_id | linked charge `id` |
| customer_ref | your internal customer ID, not the name or email |
| amount | refund amount in major units (e.g. dollars, not cents) |
| currency | ISO 4217 code, e.g. `USD` |
| status | refund `status` |
| reason | refund `reason`, or blank |

Do not include full card numbers, CVVs, or bank details. If you need to identify a payment method, use the processor's masked fields only, and only when the report requires them.
```

description: "Schedule and confirm meetings with guests outside the owner's time zone, always using the guest's local time. Use whenever a task involves creating, moving or confirming a meeting invite for an outside guest."

# Booking Meetings Across Time Zones

## The core rule
A time agreed with a guest is the time on the guest's clock. The owner's calendar is only the place the meeting is stored. Every invite, confirmation and reschedule must show the guest's local time first, with the date and time zone written out.

## Before you book
1. Find the guest's time zone from what they have said: a city, a region, a zone name such as "Pacific" or "CET", or a time they proposed with a zone. Use that.
2. If the guest has not stated a zone, do not assume it from their email domain, phone number or company location. Those can be wrong, especially for people who travel or work remotely. Ask: "What time zone are you in so I can send the right time?"
3. Write the guest's zone in the task notes before creating the invite, for example: "Guest: Dana Ruiz, Mountain Time (America/Denver)."
4. Check whether the meeting date falls on a daylight saving change for either zone. If it does, confirm the time again after the change.

## Creating the invite
1. Set the event's time zone to the guest's zone, not the owner's. Most calendar tools let you choose the zone on the event itself. Use that setting.
2. Put the agreed time in the event title or first line of the description in the guest's zone, for example: "Call with Dana Ruiz, 2:00 PM Mountain Time (Denver)."
3. Add the owner's local time in the same description line, for example: "(5:00 PM Eastern for [Owner])."
4. Do not leave the event in the owner's zone and rely on the guest's calendar to convert it. Some calendars convert wrongly or not at all.

## Verifying before you send
1. Open the saved event and read the start time as it will show for the guest's zone. Check it matches the agreed time.
2. Check the date too. A 10:00 PM Pacific slot is the next day in some zones.
3. Confirm that the owner's calendar shows the event at the right local time for the owner.
4. If any of these checks fails, fix the invite and check again before sending anything.

## Confirming with the guest
Send a short confirmation that gives the time in the guest's zone first, with the date:

> Hi Dana, confirming our call on Thursday, March 14 at 2:00 PM Mountain Time (Denver). That is 4:00 PM Eastern on [Owner]'s side. The invite is attached. If that time doesn't work for you, reply with a time that suits you and I'll adjust it.

## Moving or changing a meeting
1. When a guest asks to move a meeting, confirm the new time in the guest's zone before changing the calendar.
2. After the change, repeat the verification steps above.
3. Send an updated confirmation that replaces the old one. Say clearly that the old time is cancelled.

## When you are unsure
1. If the zone is unclear, a time looks odd, or two zones are involved, stop and ask the owner or the guest. Do not guess.
2. If a meeting has already been booked wrong and the guest may have missed it, tell the owner right away with both the wrong and correct times.

## Checklist (run through this every time)
- [ ] Guest's time zone written in the task notes
- [ ] Event time zone set to the guest's zone
- [ ] Time and date shown in the guest's zone in the event description
- [ ] Saved event checked as the guest will see it
- [ ] Confirmation sent with the guest's time first and the zone named
- [ ] Any reschedule repeats all of the above

```markdown
description: Book, reschedule, and invite external guests to meetings in the guest's own IANA timezone, never the owner's calendar default. Use for any event with at least one external attendee, and whenever a time is proposed, confirmed, or moved.
```
